first_principles_point: Built-environment upkeep is the recurring bill attached to physical civilization. A home, road, water system, store, warehouse, hospital, roof, HVAC unit, pipe, or paint layer keeps aging after it is built.
money_path: physical asset ages -> repair or replacement need -> customer budget decision -> retailer/distributor/supplier/contractor sale -> delivery -> payment -> cash conversion
company_examples: Home Depot; Lowes; Core & Main; Builders FirstSource; Sherwin-Williams; Ferguson; Watsco; Beacon; Sterling; MasTec
proof_needed: receipts; receivables; inventory turns; margin by channel; capex; debt; acquisition return
safe_use: Use as the core framing for upkeep as recurring demand, not as proof that every upkeep lane creates durable cash.

first_principles_point: Start with the roof, HVAC unit, pipe, water heater, road, or public water system. These assets do not stop deteriorating because households, cities, or businesses are under budget pressure.
money_path: asset condition -> forced or delayed maintenance choice -> purchase of materials/labor/service -> invoice -> collection
company_examples: Home Depot; Lowes; Core & Main; Sherwin-Williams; Builders FirstSource
proof_needed: repair versus discretionary split; financing evidence; household or municipal budget support; customer payment proof
safe_use: Use to explain why built assets are not one-time economic events.

first_principles_point: Time converts physical assets into future claims on cash. Deferred repair may postpone spending, but it can also raise later cost or reduce asset quality.
money_path: time passes -> wear/failure/code/weather issue -> unavoidable work -> product and labor purchase -> operating cash if payment arrives
company_examples: Home Depot; Lowes; Core & Main; Sherwin-Williams; contractors; public works suppliers
proof_needed: maintenance cadence; replacement cycles; emergency versus optional repair; OCF and FCF conversion
safe_use: Use to say physical decay creates recurring demand pressure, not that timing or margins are guaranteed.

first_principles_point: Housing affordability does not simply turn built-environment demand on or off. It changes the form of demand: fewer moves, more stuck-in-place repair, weaker large projects, more selective spending, and higher financing sensitivity.
money_path: expensive shelter -> move delayed or project resized -> repair/replacement/smaller improvement -> retailer or contractor sale -> cash if customer can pay
company_examples: Home Depot; Lowes; Builders FirstSource; Sherwin-Williams; Floor & Decor; Masco; Fortune Brands
proof_needed: ticket and traffic; Pro versus DIY mix; financing; large-project categories; repair versus remodel evidence
safe_use: Use to explain mix shift under affordability pressure without claiming housing health.

first_principles_point: When moving is unaffordable, some households spend on keeping the current home livable. That can support repair, replacement, paint, appliances, flooring, plumbing, HVAC, and Pro work.
money_path: stuck homeowner -> current-home repair/improvement -> DIY basket or contractor job -> sale -> margin -> cash
company_examples: Home Depot; Lowes; Sherwin-Williams; Masco; Fortune Brands; Floor & Decor
proof_needed: repair category sales; large-project demand; consumer financing; ticket/transaction split; customer payment evidence
safe_use: Use as a demand-substitution idea with clear limits.

first_principles_point: The Pro channel is not just larger DIY. Contractors need availability, jobsite delivery, trade credit, branches, coordination, returns, and reliability.
money_path: contractor job -> product availability/logistics -> Pro purchase or branch order -> completed work -> contractor gets paid -> distributor/retailer collects
company_examples: Home Depot SRS/GMS; Lowes Pro; Core & Main; Builders FirstSource; Sherwin-Williams Paint Stores; Ferguson; Watsco; Beacon
proof_needed: Pro sales mix; Pro margin; receivables aging; trade credit; delivery cost; contractor retention
safe_use: Use to explain why Pro infrastructure can matter while keeping credit and margin boundaries explicit.

first_principles_point: Civic systems are built-environment upkeep even when consumers do not see them. Water, wastewater, storm drainage, fire protection, treatment plants, and roads age in the background.
money_path: aging civic asset -> project need -> funding/procurement -> contractor order -> distributor sale -> delivery -> invoice -> receivable collection
company_examples: Core & Main; Ferguson; Mueller Water; Xylem; Jacobs; Sterling; MasTec; Quanta; United Rentals; Vulcan; Martin Marietta
proof_needed: funded project evidence; municipal receipts; procurement timing; category margin; receivables; inventory; branch economics
safe_use: Use to show civic infrastructure as a hidden upkeep lane, not as automatic funded cash.

first_principles_point: Every built-environment story has embedded materials: lumber, coatings, pipe, fittings, aggregates, asphalt, cement, steel, HVAC, plumbing, fixtures, tools, and chemicals.
money_path: raw input or manufactured material -> supplier/distributor inventory -> project sale -> price pass-through or margin squeeze -> cash impact
company_examples: Sherwin-Williams; Builders FirstSource; West Fraser; Nucor; Steel Dynamics; Vulcan; Martin Marietta; Owens Corning; Carlisle; PPG
proof_needed: price versus volume; gross margin drivers; raw-material cost; inventory timing; pass-through evidence
safe_use: Use to connect upkeep to commodity pressure while separating demand from cash quality.

first_principles_point: Upkeep demand is limited by people who can do the work. Labor scarcity turns into cost, delay, quality risk, and demand for productivity systems.
money_path: labor scarcity or job complexity -> need for productivity support -> prefab/delivery/digital/branch support -> higher-value sale -> cash if execution works
company_examples: Builders FirstSource; Home Depot; Lowes; Core & Main; Sherwin-Williams; United Rentals; Quanta; MasTec; Sterling; Jacobs
proof_needed: labor cost; project delays; value-added margin; prefab adoption; contractor productivity; execution quality
safe_use: Use to show labor as a real economic constraint, not just a hiring issue.

first_principles_point: Companies try to control more of the route from physical need to completed work through branches, stores, delivery, acquisitions, contractor accounts, and specialized distribution.
money_path: fragmented local demand -> owned branch/store/distribution platform -> more capture -> sale -> integration and working-capital test -> cash
company_examples: Home Depot SRS/GMS; Lowes FBM/ADG; Core & Main acquisitions; Sherwin-Williams stores; Builders FirstSource locations; Ferguson; Beacon; SiteOne; Watsco
proof_needed: acquisition contribution; integration cost; branch profitability; inventory; receivables; delivery cost; ROIC
safe_use: Use to explain why distribution control can be strategic only if it converts into cash.

first_principles_point: Built-environment demand is local in execution. Weather, housing age, income, insurance, permitting, municipal finances, water quality, labor, and local growth decide the actual cash path.
money_path: local asset condition and local budget -> branch/store/contractor order -> delivery -> invoice -> local collection
company_examples: Home Depot; Lowes; Core & Main; Sherwin-Williams; Builders FirstSource; Sterling; MasTec; local contractors
proof_needed: regional sales; branch performance; local funding; weather impact; insurance impact; permit timing; collection evidence
safe_use: Use to avoid treating a national theme as identical in every market.

safe_use: Use to explain why upkeep is a societal affordability problem, not only an investment screen.
